description_full: Accel Entertainment, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, operates as a distributed gaming operator in the United States. It engages in the installation, maintenance, and operation of gaming terminals; redemption devices that disburse winnings and contain automated teller machine (ATM) functionality; and other amusement devices in authorized non-casino locations, such as restaurants, bars, taverns, convenience stores, liquor stores, truck stops, and grocery stores. The company also designs and manufactures gaming terminals and related equipment, as well as offers turnkey and full-service gaming solutions to bars, restaurants, convenience stores, truck stops, and fraternal and veteran establishments. In addition, it operates stand-alone ATMs in gaming and non-gaming locations, as well as amusement devices, including jukeboxes, dartboards, pool tables, and other entertainment related equipment; and develops brick-and-mortar casinos that serve local gaming markets and horse racing venues. Accel Entertainment, Inc. is headquartered in Burr Ridge, Illinois.

financial_summary: Accel Entertainment, Inc. is a small-cap consumer cyclical business with a $1.1B market cap on $1.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +11% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 16% against a 7% cost of capital, a 9-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $62M in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.93× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -9.0% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.9× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 3.4×.

Shareholder yield of 3.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 15% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 2% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 35% and a beta of 0.71, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.01 vs 5y 0.61), so read it loosely.

val: The stock trades 59% below its DCF fair value of $33.30, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 21%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $22.38 to $50.48 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Consumer Cyclical peers: EV/EBITDA 6.8 vs 11.2 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 14% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.6% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.8% (vs the 8% bar).

prof: ROIC of 16% clears the cost of capital of 7.0% by 9pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.58).
It converts 5% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is mixed: cash conversion of 2.93x, but high accruals (-9.0% of assets).
ROE of 19% is amplified by 4.1x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 0.9% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.9x net debt to EBITDA ($296.6M of cash against $607.4M of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 3.4x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 11.1% over 3 years and 33.3% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 50%).
At current returns, reinvesting 52% of profits supports about 8.2% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Capex runs 1.7x depreciation (6.7% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 37, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 21.0% on average.
own: Insiders own 14.6%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 78%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (7 sales, net $1.5M sold).
It returns 3.6% a year to shareholders (3.6% in buybacks).
people: With about 1,600 employees, each generates about $832K of revenue, 2.2x the Consumer Cyclical median.
That works out to $39K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $873K (1x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
